docs.title: poincare-memory
docs.text:
Hierarchy-aware, time-aware memory for LLM agents and RAG, on the Poincaré ball.

Flat vector stores put every memory in Euclidean space, where a hierarchy of a few thousand concepts has nowhere to go. Hyperbolic space has exponentially more room near its boundary, which is exactly the shape of a hierarchy. poincare-memory places each memory in the Poincaré ball with its direction from the text embedding and its depth from its place in the hierarchy, weights it by age at query time, answers structural questions (subtree, ancestors, siblings, entailment cones) geometrically, and lets you see all of it in one self-contained HTML file.

It is the official open-source reference implementation of the geometry-aware memory component of

D. Mojila, "LLM Orchestration with Geometry-Aware Memory," 2026 2nd International Conference on Big Data & Machine Learning (ICBDML), Bhopal, India, Feb. 2026, pp. 1–7. doi:10.1109/ICBDML68582.2026.11544690

Provenance

This package was written after the paper, from the paper's description and the primary literature. The system used for the paper's experiments is not released, and every number in these docs comes from code in this repository.

docs.title: In one minute
docs.text:
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
from poincare_memory import Memory, HalfLife

mem = Memory(decay=HalfLife(hours=24 * 30))  # observations fade with a 30-day half-life

body = mem.add("Human musculoskeletal system")
lower = mem.add("Lower limb musculature", parent=body)
hams = mem.add("Hamstring group: knee flexion and hip extension", parent=lower)
bf = mem.add("Biceps femoris: lateral hamstring", parent=hams)
mem.add(
    "Athlete A reported tight hamstrings after 400 m repeats",
    parent=hams,
    t=datetime.now(timezone.utc) - timedelta(days=30),
)

for r in mem.search("hamstring tightness", k=3):
    print(f"{r.score:6.2f}  depth={r.depth:.1f}  w={r.time_weight:.2f}  {r.text}")

mem.search("knee", mode="subtree", root=lower)  # only the lower-limb branch
mem.search(mode="ancestors", root=bf)  # hams → lower → body
mem.inspect("memory.html")  # interactive disk, table and tree
mem.save("memory.db")  # one SQLite file

docs.title: poincare_memory.store.memory.Memory
docs.text:
Memory(
    embedder=None,
    curvature=1.0,
    decay=None,
    base_depth=1.0,
    depth_step=0.5,
    inherit=0.25,
    cone_constrained=False,
    cone_k=DEFAULT_K,
    metric="shell",
    time_coef=1.0,
    depth_bias=0.0,
    clock=None,
)

Hierarchy-aware, time-aware memory for agents and RAG.

Each memory gets a point in the Poincaré ball. Its direction comes from the text embedding (optionally pulled toward its parent's direction); its depth (hyperbolic distance from the origin) comes from its level in the hierarchy you declare with parent=. Structural queries (subtree, ancestors, siblings, cone) and the temporal policy are geometric and explicit, and every memory can be inspected visually.

Scoring. search ranks memories by -distance + depth_bias * depth + time_coef * log(time_weight). With metric="shell" (default) distance is the hyperbolic distance between the query and the memory after both are moved to the reference shell at base_depth: it measures semantic (angular) mismatch in hyperbolic units and is comparable across levels. With metric="hyperbolic" it is the raw distance to the memory's actual point, which strongly favours shallow, general memories (a root at depth 1 is close to everything) and is the right choice only when the embedder itself is hyperbolic (e.g. Hierarchy Transformers) or when generality is wanted. Use depth_bias to prefer specific (> 0) or general (< 0) memories explicitly.

Thread safety. All mutating and searching methods take an internal re-entrant lock, so a Memory can be shared between threads; the embedder you pass must be safe to call from several threads if you do.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default embedder Embedder | None

Anything with dim and embed(texts); defaults to the offline :class:~poincare_memory.embed.HashingEmbedder.

None curvature float

Positive curvature magnitude c of the ball.

1.0 decay DecayPolicy | None

Temporal policy; defaults to :class:~poincare_memory.temporal.NoDecay.

None base_depth float

Hyperbolic radius of root memories and the extra radius per level.

1.0 depth_step float

Hyperbolic radius of root memories and the extra radius per level.

1.0 inherit float

How much of the parent's direction a child inherits (0 = none, 1 = all).

0.25 cone_constrained bool

Force children inside the parent's entailment cone. Makes cone queries exact for the declared hierarchy but collapses semantic directions onto a few rays; off by default.

False cone_k float

The K constant of entailment cones (Ganea et al. 2018).

DEFAULT_K metric Metric

Default distance for search; see above.

'shell' time_coef float

Score weights; see :func:poincare_memory.retrieval.combine.

1.0 depth_bias float

Score weights; see :func:poincare_memory.retrieval.combine.

1.0 clock Callable[[], datetime] | None

Callable returning "now"; override in tests or simulations.

None

docs.title: search
docs.text:
search(
    query=None,
    k=5,
    mode="nearest",
    root=None,
    at_time=None,
    filters=None,
    metric=None,
    query_depth=None,
    touch=True,
    use_index=None,
    oversample=8,
)

Rank memories by -distance + depth_bias*depth + time_coef*log(time_weight).

mode restricts the candidates: nearest (all), subtree/children/ ancestors/siblings of root, or cone (points inside the entailment cone of root). query may be omitted for structural modes, in which case candidates are ranked by time weight and depth only. metric overrides the memory's default (see the class docstring); query_depth only matters for metric="hyperbolic" (default base_depth).

use_index: with True (or None once :meth:build_index has been called) a nearest + shell search first takes the k * oversample closest memories from the index, then scores them exactly with the temporal policy and filters. The index is rebuilt automatically after changes.

docs.title: poincare_memory.geometry.lorentz
docs.text:
Lorentz (hyperboloid) model helpers.

The hyperboloid of curvature -c is {X in R^{d+1} : <X, X>_L = -1/c, X_0 > 0} with the Lorentzian inner product <X, Y>_L = -X_0 Y_0 + sum_i X_i Y_i.

Why it matters for retrieval: the geodesic distance is d(X, Y) = (1/sqrt(c)) arcosh(-c <X, Y>_L), a decreasing function of the Lorentzian inner product. Negating the time coordinate of every stored vector turns <X, Y>_L into an ordinary dot product, so any maximum-inner-product (dot-product) ANN index returns exact hyperbolic nearest neighbours. This is the trick used by hyperbolic RAG systems and documented by vector-database vendors; no custom metric is needed.

docs.title: HashingEmbedder dataclass
docs.text:
HashingEmbedder(dim=256, ngram_range=(3, 5), seed=0)

Deterministic, dependency-free text embedder (word + character n-gram hashing).

It is not a semantic model; it is a stable, fast stand-in that makes the library usable offline and in tests. Swap in :class:SentenceTransformerEmbedder or any callable for real semantics.

Algorithm (stable across versions and ports): lower-case the text; tokens are [\w']+; features are "w:" + token and "c:" + ngram for character n-grams of "#" + token + "#" with lengths in ngram_range; each feature is hashed with keyed BLAKE2b (digest 8 bytes, key = 4-byte little-endian seed); index = first 4 bytes as little-endian integer mod dim; sign = +1 if the fifth byte is odd else -1; the row is L2-normalised.

docs.title: poincare_memory.hierarchy.sarkar
docs.text:
Training-free tree embedding by Sarkar's combinatorial construction.

Sarkar (2011) showed that any tree embeds in the hyperbolic plane with arbitrarily low distortion: put the root at the origin, place its children on a circle of hyperbolic radius tau at evenly spaced angles, then for every child move it to the origin by an isometry, place its own children on a circle around it while avoiding the direction of its parent, and move everything back. Sala, De Sa, Gu & Ré (ICML 2018) analysed the construction and extended it to higher dimensions by spreading child directions on a sphere.

This module implements both from the papers. Larger tau lowers distortion but pushes deep nodes toward the boundary; :func:max_safe_depth tells you how deep a tree can go before floating-point projection starts compressing it.

docs.title: max_safe_depth
docs.text:
max_safe_depth(ball, tau, dtype=np.float64)

Largest total hyperbolic radius representable before the ball margin clips points.

Returns the number of tau-length steps from the origin that stay strictly inside (1 - eps) / sqrt(c).

docs.title: spread_directions
docs.text:
spread_directions(
    k, dim, avoid=None, seed=0, iterations=200
)

k unit vectors in R^dim spread apart (and away from avoid if given).

In two dimensions the angles are exact: children fill the circle evenly, with the parent's direction occupying one slot. In higher dimensions a seeded repulsion on the sphere (a Thomson-style relaxation) spreads the directions.

docs.title: sarkar_layout
docs.text:
sarkar_layout(
    edges,
    ball=None,
    dim=2,
    tau=1.0,
    edge_length=None,
    root=None,
    seed=0,
)

Embed a rooted tree given as (parent, child) edges.

Every child is placed at hyperbolic distance tau * edge_length[(parent, child)] from its parent (edge_length defaults to 1). Returns node -> point. A forest is handled by treating the listed root (or the single root) as the origin; pass a virtual root edge set if you have several roots.

docs.title: poincare_memory.hierarchy.rsgd
docs.text:
Poincaré embeddings trained with Riemannian SGD (Nickel & Kiela, NeurIPS 2017), in NumPy.

Use this when the hierarchy is noisy, partial, or a DAG rather than a tree; for a clean tree :func:~poincare_memory.hierarchy.sarkar.sarkar_layout is exact and instantaneous. A Euclidean twin with the same loss is provided as a baseline for benchmarks. Implemented from the paper; no third-party code was consulted.

docs.title: reconstruction
docs.text:
reconstruction(points, closure, distance)

Reconstruction protocol of Nickel & Kiela (2017).

For every node u with related nodes R(u): the mean rank of each related node counts only unrelated nodes that are closer to u (so hub nodes with many descendants are not penalised for their own descendants), and the average precision is computed over the ranking of all other nodes.

docs.title: poincare_memory.temporal.policies
docs.text:
Named temporal weighting policies.

The paper describes "time-weighted embeddings" that favour recent information while keeping established knowledge reachable. Here that idea is a pluggable, testable policy that maps a memory's age (and optionally its access history or validity window) to a weight in (0, 1]. Weights enter the retrieval score as time_coef * log(weight), so a weight of 1 is neutral.

Forms implemented from the literature: - exponential half-life (the 0.995^hours recency of Generative Agents, Park et al. 2023, is HalfLife(hours=138.3)); - Ebbinghaus forgetting exp(-t / S) with stability that grows with accesses (MemoryBank, Zhong et al. 2024); - validity windows (bi-temporal facts as in Graphiti/Zep).

docs.title: poincare_memory.retrieval.scoring
docs.text: Combining geometry and time into one retrieval score.

docs.title: combine
docs.text:
combine(
    distances,
    time_weights=None,
    depths=None,
    time_coef=1.0,
    depth_bias=0.0,
)

score = -distance + depth_bias * depth + time_coef * log(time_weight).

Larger is better. depth_bias > 0 prefers specific (deep) memories, < 0 prefers general ones; time_coef scales how strongly the temporal policy counts (1.0 means a half-life halving of the weight costs ln 2 in score, the same as moving ln 2 ≈ 0.69 further away in the ball).

docs.title: poincare_memory.retrieval.cones
docs.text:
Hyperbolic entailment cones (Ganea, Bécigneul & Hofmann, ICML 2018).

Every point x in the ball (outside a small central region of radius K) owns a geodesically convex cone opening toward the boundary. "y lies in the cone of x" is the geometric form of "x entails / is more general than y". With depth encoded by the norm, cones give ancestor and descendant queries that plain nearest-neighbour search cannot express.

Formulas (unit ball; points are scaled by sqrt(c) first): half-aperture psi(x) = arcsin(K (1 - ||x||^2) / ||x||) angle at x Xi(x, y) = arccos( ((1 + ||x||^2) - ||x||^2 (1 + ||y||^2)) / (||x|| ||x - y|| sqrt(1 + ||x||^2 ||y||^2 - 2)) ) energy E(x, y) = max(0, Xi(x, y) - psi(x)) (0 means y is inside the cone)

docs.title: cone_energy
docs.text:
cone_energy(x, y, ball, K=DEFAULT_K)

max(0, Xi(x, y) - psi(x)); zero when y is inside the entailment cone of x.

docs.title: poincare_memory.index
docs.text:
Nearest-neighbour indexes for the reference-shell metric.

Semantic search in :class:~poincare_memory.Memory compares the query with every memory on the root shell. For large stores that comparison is offloaded to a maximum-inner-product index: shell points are mapped to the Lorentz model and their time coordinate negated (:func:~poincare_memory.geometry.to_mips_vectors), after which the largest dot products are exactly the hyperbolic nearest neighbours. Two backends:

  • numpy: exact, vectorised, fine to a few hundred thousand points;
  • faiss: IndexHNSWFlat with inner-product metric (pip install poincare-memory[ann]), approximate, for millions of points.

2-D Poincaré-disk coordinates for drawing.

In 2-D the points are returned unchanged (scaled to the unit disk). In higher dimensions the directions are reduced with an uncentred SVD of the tangent vectors at the origin (so the origin stays the origin) and every point keeps its exact hyperbolic depth; angles are approximate, depths are not.

docs.title: structural_coordinates
docs.text:
structural_coordinates(memory)

2-D disk coordinates for inspection: angles from the hierarchy, radii from the true depths.

Every memory keeps its exact hyperbolic distance from the origin (the paper's depth coordinate); its angle comes from a radial tree layout in which each subtree owns an angular wedge proportional to its number of leaves, so siblings spread evenly and subtrees do not overlap. This is a drawing, not an isometric embedding: use the real points for distances.

docs.title: WordNet reconstruction
docs.text:
Protocol (Nickel & Kiela 2017): take the transitive closure of a WordNet noun sub-hierarchy, embed its nodes, and for every node rank all other nodes by distance; report mean average precision and mean rank of the related nodes. Run:

pip install "poincare-memory[bench]"
python benchmarks/wordnet_reconstruction.py --subtree mammal.n.01 --dims 2 5 10 --epochs 200 --lr 0.3

The script trains the Poincaré and Euclidean embeddings with the same loss, sampling and epochs, and prints a table. Latest run (2026-10-10, 200 epochs, lr 0.3, mammal.n.01 with 1,170 nodes):

dim Poincaré MAP Euclidean MAP 2 0.779 0.533 5 0.975 0.802 10 0.957 0.837

Numbers are only published once produced by this script; benchmarks/README.md has the full table with mean ranks, the environment and the raw JSON.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Poincaré ball geometry with curvature (distance, distance_arcosh, exp/log maps, Möbius operations, Lorentz conversions, dot-product trick for ANN indexes), float32/float64.
  • Memory: hierarchy-aware, time-aware store with structural search modes (subtree, children, ancestors, siblings, cone), named temporal policies, SQLite persistence.
  • Visual inspection: self-contained interactive HTML (disk, table, tree), matplotlib plot, Jupyter rendering, ASCII tree, DataFrame export.
  • Sarkar's training-free tree layout (2-D exact, n-D spread) with a float64 depth safety check; Riemannian SGD Poincaré embeddings and a Euclidean baseline; reconstruction MAP / mean rank.
  • Offline hashing embedder, Sentence-Transformers wrapper, callable adapter.
  • Inspector layouts: structural (radial tree at true hyperbolic depths, default when parents exist) and projection (semantic directions); DecayPolicy exported at package level.
  • WordNet mammals benchmark results recorded with raw JSON and a chart; README demo GIF.
  • Production hardening: add_many (one embedding call), update, to_json / from_json, stats, __repr__, input validation, module logging, a re-entrant lock around all mutating and searching calls, and build_index with NumPy or FAISS ([ann] extra) backends for indexed shell-metric search; SearchResult.to_dict; CLI stats, export, import.
  • Documentation site (mkdocs-material): getting started, concepts, eight guides, API reference, FAQ; every Python block in the docs is executed in CI by scripts/check_docs_examples.py.
  • The hashing embedder now keys BLAKE2b with the seed (instead of salting), so the TypeScript port in the explainer produces identical vectors.
  • CLI (demo, inspect, tree, search), WordNet reconstruction benchmark, documentation.

docs.title: The ball
docs.text:
The Poincaré ball of curvature \(-c\) is the open ball of radius \(1/\sqrt{c}\) with the metric tensor \(g_x = \big(\tfrac{2}{1 - c\|x\|^2}\big)^2 g^E\) (the paper's eq. 2 with \(c = 1\)). Distances grow without bound near the boundary, and the circumference of a hyperbolic circle of radius \(r\) grows like \(\sinh r\): a tree with branching factor \(b\) needs room that grows like \(b^{\text{depth}}\), and that is exactly what hyperbolic space supplies (Sarkar 2011; Sala, De Sa, Gu and Ré 2018).

The distance between two points is the paper's eq. 3,

\[ d(x, y) = \operatorname{arcosh}\Big(1 + \frac{2\,\|x - y\|^2}{(1 - \|x\|^2)(1 - \|y\|^2)}\Big), \]

implemented as PoincareBall.distance_arcosh; the gyrovector form \((2/\sqrt{c})\,\operatorname{artanh}(\sqrt{c}\,\|(-x) \oplus_c y\|)\) is PoincareBall.distance. Both agree to \(10^{-8}\) in the test suite. Exponential and logarithmic maps, Möbius addition, the conformal factor, and conversions to and from the Lorentz model are all in poincare_memory.geometry.

docs.title: Depth and direction
docs.text:
Every memory's point has two independent components.

  • Depth: the hyperbolic distance from the origin. Roots sit at base_depth; every level adds depth_step. Depth is read back from the geometry (Memory.depth(id)), not from a table, and it is the paper's "distance from the centre encodes hierarchy".
  • Direction: from the text embedding, L2-normalised, then pulled toward the parent's direction along the geodesic by the fraction inherit (default 0.25). Inheritance makes siblings cluster and keeps branches angularly coherent without erasing what each memory is about.

cone_constrained=True additionally forces each child inside its parent's entailment cone. That makes cone queries exact for the declared hierarchy but collapses semantic directions onto a few rays, so it is off by default; the explicit hierarchy serves subtree and ancestors instead.

docs.title: Entailment cones
docs.text: Ganea, Bécigneul and Hofmann (2018) attach to each point \(x\) (outside a small central region of radius \(K\)) a geodesically convex cone opening toward the boundary, with half-aperture \(\psi(x) = \arcsin\big(K(1 - \|x\|^2)/\|x\|\big)\). "\(y\) lies in the cone of \(x\)" is the geometric form of "\(x\) is more general than \(y\)", and cones are transitive. mode="cone" returns the memories inside a memory's cone, ranked by score; cone_energy gives the violation angle.

docs.title: Time
docs.text:
The paper's "time-weighted embeddings" are a pluggable policy mapping a memory's age (and optionally its access history or validity window) to a weight in \((0, 1]\):

Policy Weight From HalfLife(hours) \(0.5^{\Delta t / h}\) the \(0.995^{\text{hours}}\) recency of Generative Agents is generative_agents_recency() Ebbinghaus(stability_hours, boost_per_access) \(e^{-\Delta t / S}\), \(S\) grows with accesses MemoryBank's forgetting curve ValidityWindow() 1 inside [valid_from, valid_until], tiny outside bi-temporal facts (Graphiti/Zep) Product(p1, p2, …) elementwise product combine them

Weights enter the score as \(\text{time\_coef} \cdot \ln w\), so a halving of the weight costs \(\ln 2\), the same as moving \(0.69\) further away in the ball. search(at_time=…) evaluates the policy at any moment.

docs.title: Scoring
docs.text:
search ranks by

\[ \text{score} = -\,d + \text{depth\_bias}\cdot\text{depth} + \text{time\_coef}\cdot\ln w . \]

docs.title: Why the reference shell
docs.text:
With fixed text embeddings, raw hyperbolic distance between a query and the stored points is biased toward shallow memories. From a query on the root shell (depth 1), a root memory 90° away is at distance 1.51. A memory at depth 3 is at least 2.0 away at any angle, so it never wins; a memory at depth 2 wins only within 36.5° of the query's direction, one at depth 1.5 only within 60°. (For large depths the distance approaches \(D_q + D_m + 2\ln\sin(\theta/2)\); at the default depths that approximation is not accurate.) Measured on the bundled demo, raw distance returned the root for all ten keyword queries and for 13 of the 32 memories' own texts.

metric="shell" therefore moves both the query and the memory to the root shell before measuring, so \(d\) is semantic mismatch in hyperbolic units and is comparable across levels. Depth enters explicitly through depth_bias (prefer specific memories with \(> 0\), general ones with \(< 0\)) and through the structural modes. This is how the implementation realises the paper's "similarity measures that account for both semantic content and structural relationships".

metric="hyperbolic" keeps the raw distance to the memory's actual point and is the right choice when the embedder is itself hyperbolic (for example Hierarchy Transformers), or when generality is what you want.

docs.title: Training-free versus learned placement
docs.text:
Memory.add places points deterministically from the embedding and the declared parent, which is what an agent needs at write time. For analysis you can also embed a whole hierarchy at once:

  • sarkar_layout(edges) places a tree exactly by Sarkar's construction (children on a circle of hyperbolic radius \(\tau\) around each node, avoiding the parent's direction), with a float64 safety check max_safe_depth;
  • fit_poincare_embeddings(closure) learns points by Riemannian SGD on the transitive closure (Nickel and Kiela 2017), with fit_euclidean_embeddings as the same-loss baseline and reconstruction() for MAP and mean rank.

docs.title: Any vector database
docs.text: Map points to the Lorentz model and negate the time coordinate (to_lorentz, to_mips_vectors): the dot product with a query's Lorentz vector is then exactly its Lorentzian inner product, a decreasing function of hyperbolic distance, so any maximum-inner-product index returns exact hyperbolic nearest neighbours. Memory.build_index() does this for the reference shell with a NumPy or FAISS backend; see Scaling.

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text:
Is this the system from the paper? No. It is the author's open-source reference implementation of the memory component, written after the paper from its description and the primary literature. The system used for the paper's experiments is not released, and every number here comes from this repository's code.

Do I need a GPU or a service? No. The core is NumPy; the default embedder runs offline; persistence is one SQLite or JSON file.

Why not just rank by hyperbolic distance? Because a point near the centre is close to everything. See Concepts → Scoring; the raw metric is available as metric="hyperbolic".

How deep can a hierarchy go? About twenty levels with the defaults (base_depth=1, depth_step=0.5) before float64 runs out of room near the boundary; max_safe_depth tells you the limit for your settings, and sarkar_layout warns when a tree would exceed it.

Can I use my own vector database? Yes; see Scaling: a dot product on Lorentz-mapped vectors is an exact hyperbolic nearest-neighbour search.

Is it thread-safe? Yes for one process: every mutating and searching call takes an internal re-entrant lock. Your embedder must be safe to call concurrently if you share a Memory across threads.

What about the orchestration part of the paper? poincare-orchestra implements the controller, ensemble and synthesis on top of this memory.

How do I cite it? Cite the paper (BibTeX in the README) and, for the software, the Zenodo release listed in CITATION.cff.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install poincare-memory                 # NumPy only, runs offline
pip install "poincare-memory[embed]"        # + Sentence-Transformers embedder
pip install "poincare-memory[viz,pandas]"   # + matplotlib plot, DataFrame export
pip install "poincare-memory[ann]"          # + FAISS index for large stores

Python 3.10 or newer. No services, no GPU. For development, see Contributing.

docs.title: A first memory
docs.text:
from poincare_memory import Memory

mem = Memory()
support = mem.add("Support knowledge base", id="kb")
api = mem.add("Public API: authentication, rate limits, pagination", parent="kb", id="api")
mem.add("API rate limit is 250 requests per second per project", parent="api", id="rate")
mem.add("Tokens expire after 60 minutes", parent="api", id="tokens")
print(mem)
print(mem.tree())

Memory(n=4, dim=256, curvature=1, decay=NoDecay(), metric='shell')
Support knowledge base  [kb d=1.00]
└── Public API: authentication, rate limits, pagination  [api d=1.50]
    ├── API rate limit is 250 requests per second per project  [rate d=2.00]
    └── Tokens expire after 60 minutes  [tokens d=2.00]

Three things happened on each add:

  1. the text was embedded (by default with the offline hashing embedder; swap in a real model for real semantics);
  2. the point's direction came from that embedding, pulled a quarter of the way toward its parent's direction;
  3. the point's depth, its hyperbolic distance from the origin, was set to the parent's depth plus depth_step (roots sit at base_depth). The d= values in the tree are those depths.

docs.title: A first search
docs.text:
for r in mem.search("how fast can I call the API", k=2):
    print(f"{r.score:+.3f}  distance={r.distance:.3f}  depth={r.depth:.2f}  {r.id}: {r.text}")

Scores are -distance + depth_bias * depth + time_coef * log(time_weight). With the default settings only the distance counts, and it is measured on the reference shell: the query and the memory are both moved to the root depth so that the number reflects semantic mismatch only (why).

Structural questions do not need a query:

mem.search(mode="children", root="api")  # rate, tokens
mem.search(mode="ancestors", root="rate")  # api, kb
mem.search("limits", mode="subtree", root="api", k=5)

docs.title: Time
docs.text:
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
from poincare_memory import HalfLife

now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
mem = Memory(decay=HalfLife(hours=24 * 7))
mem.add("Release 2.3: rate limit 100 rps", id="old", t=now - timedelta(days=60))
mem.add("Release 2.4: rate limit 250 rps", id="new", t=now - timedelta(days=2))
print([r.id for r in mem.search("rate limit", k=2)])  # ['new', 'old']
print([r.id for r in mem.search("rate limit", k=2, at_time=now - timedelta(days=50))])  # the past

Facts that stop being true on a date get a valid_until and a ValidityWindow policy; see Time and forgetting.

docs.title: A first picture
docs.text:
mem.inspect("memory.html")  # add open_browser=True to open it

One self-contained file: an interactive Poincaré disk (hover, click to light up ancestors and descendants, drag to pan hyperbolically, slide time), a sortable table and a collapsible tree. In Jupyter, a Memory renders the same inspector inline. See Inspecting a memory.

docs.title: Persist
docs.text:
mem.save("memory.db")
again = Memory.load("memory.db")
mem.to_json("memory.json")

poincare-memory demo -o demo --open       # build the anatomy demo, save demo.db, open demo.html

docs.title: Mapping to the paper
docs.text:
Paper Code §III-A Poincaré ball, metric tensor, distance (eq. 1–3) geometry/poincare.py §IV-C structured knowledge representation Memory.add(parent=…), hierarchy/sarkar.py, hierarchy/rsgd.py §IV-C temporal context management temporal/policies.py, Memory.search(at_time=…) §IV-C efficient retrieval mechanisms Memory.search(mode=…), retrieval/cones.py, geometry/lorentz.py §IV-C cross-domain knowledge integration several roots in one Memory §IV-B controller, §IV-D ensemble, §IV-E synthesis companion package poincare-orchestra

This is a reference implementation written from the paper's description; the evaluation in the paper used a system that is not part of this repository.

docs.title: Using it in an agent
docs.text:
A memory layer has two moments: write and read.

from datetime import datetime, timezone
from poincare_memory import Ebbinghaus, Memory

mem = Memory(decay=Ebbinghaus(stability_hours=24 * 7, boost_per_access=0.5))
athlete = mem.add("Athlete profile: 400 m sprinter, 24, right-leg dominant", id="athlete")
mem.add("Injury history", parent=athlete, id="injury")
mem.add("Training log", parent=athlete, id="log")


def observe(text: str, where: str) -> str:
    """Write: attach an observation under the right branch."""
    return mem.add(text, parent=where, t=datetime.now(timezone.utc))


def context(question: str, k: int = 4) -> str:
    """Read: time-weighted, hierarchy-aware context for the model."""
    hits = mem.search(question, k=k)  # accesses strengthen stability
    return "\n".join(f"- [{h.id}] ({h.time_weight:.2f}) {h.text}" for h in hits)


observe("Calf tightness after hill sprints", "log")
observe("Grade 1 hamstring strain, left, 2025-11", "injury")
print(context("how is the athlete's hamstring?"))

Patterns that work well:

  • Structural nodes are timeless, observations are dated. Give branches no decay by dating them "now" or by filtering on meta; let observations carry real timestamps.
  • Route by branch. When you know the topic, search mode="subtree" under it first and fall back to global search; the companion package poincare-orchestra does exactly this per sub-task.
  • Let validity windows retire facts instead of deleting them, so the past stays reconstructible with at_time.
  • Inspect before you trust. mem.inspect() shows what the agent knows; mem.stats() shows how old it is.
  • Persist per user or per session with save(); reload with the same embedder.

The orchestration side of the paper, with a metacognitive controller, provider-agnostic ensemble and multi-objective synthesis, is implemented in poincare-orchestra.

docs.title: Embedders
docs.text: An embedder is anything with a dim and an embed(texts) -> array of shape (n, dim).

docs.title: The offline hashing embedder (default)
docs.text: HashingEmbedder(dim=256) hashes word and character n-gram features with keyed BLAKE2b into a fixed-size vector and L2-normalises it. It is deterministic, dependency-free and fast, which keeps the library usable offline and in tests, but it is not a semantic model: it matches on shared words and sub-words, not meaning. Its exact algorithm is documented in the class docstring and ported to TypeScript in the explainer, so vectors are identical across languages.

docs.title: Sentence-Transformers
docs.text:
# docs: skip (downloads a model)
from poincare_memory import Memory, SentenceTransformerEmbedder

mem = Memory(embedder=SentenceTransformerEmbedder("sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2"))

pip install "poincare-memory[embed]". Vectors are L2-normalised; the direction is all the memory uses.

docs.title: Any callable
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from poincare_memory import CallableEmbedder, Memory


def my_encode(texts):  # stand-in for any model or API call
    rng = np.random.default_rng(abs(hash(tuple(texts))) % 2**32)
    return rng.normal(size=(len(texts), 1024))


emb = CallableEmbedder(fn=my_encode, dim=1024)
mem = Memory(embedder=emb)
mem.add("works with any vector source")

API embedders (OpenAI, Cohere, Voyage, …) fit this shape; batch them, because add_many sends all texts in one call.

docs.title: Hyperbolic encoders
docs.text: Hierarchy Transformers (He et al. 2024, pip install hierarchy-transformers) produce points that already live in a Poincaré ball of radius \(\sqrt{d}\). To use them natively, construct the ball with the matching curvature (Memory(curvature=1/d, ...)), feed the raw outputs through a CallableEmbedder, and search with metric="hyperbolic".

docs.title: Persistence note
docs.text: Memory.load and Memory.from_json restore the hashing embedder automatically. For any other embedder, pass the same instance to load; the saved dimension is checked against it.

docs.title: Parents first
docs.text:
A memory's depth comes from its parent, so parents must exist before children. Give stable ids to structural nodes so you can refer to them later:

from poincare_memory import Memory

mem = Memory()
mem.add_many(
    [
        {"text": "Human musculoskeletal system", "id": "body"},
        {"text": "Lower limb musculature", "parent": "body", "id": "lower"},
        {
            "text": "Hamstring group: knee flexion and hip extension",
            "parent": "lower",
            "id": "hams",
        },
        {"text": "Biceps femoris: lateral hamstring", "parent": "hams", "id": "bf"},
        {"text": "Semitendinosus: medial hamstring", "parent": "hams", "id": "st"},
    ]
)
print(mem.level("bf"), round(mem.depth("bf"), 2))  # 3 2.5

add_many embeds all texts in one call, which matters with real embedding models.

docs.title: Several roots
docs.text: A memory can hold several independent hierarchies; each root sits at base_depth with its own direction. mem.roots() lists them, and search runs across all of them unless you restrict it with mode="subtree".

docs.title: Depth settings
docs.text: base_depth (default 1.0) and depth_step (default 0.5) are hyperbolic units. Points must stay inside the float64-safe radius, about 12 units for curvature 1 (max_safe_depth), so with the defaults you have room for roughly twenty levels. A larger depth_step spreads levels further apart, which strengthens the separation structural modes see and weakens nothing in the shell metric.

docs.title: Re-parenting, updating, removing
docs.text:
mem.link("st", "lower")  # move a subtree; depths and directions are recomputed
mem.update("hams", text="Hamstrings: knee flexion and hip extension", meta={"source": "textbook"})
mem.remove("st")  # leaves only; pass cascade=True to drop a subtree

update with new text re-embeds the memory and re-places its descendants, because their directions inherit from it.

docs.title: Inspecting the structure
docs.text:
print(mem.tree())
print(mem.ancestors("bf"), mem.descendants("lower"), mem.siblings("bf"))
print(mem.stats()["levels"])

docs.title: Embedding a whole tree at once
docs.text: When you have a complete taxonomy rather than a stream of memories, sarkar_layout gives an exact, training-free embedding and fit_poincare_embeddings a learned one; see Concepts and Benchmarks.

docs.title: Inspecting a memory
docs.text: Seeing is the point of putting memories in a disk.

docs.title: The HTML inspector
docs.text:
from poincare_memory.demo import build_demo_memory

mem = build_demo_memory()
html = mem.inspect("memory.html", title="my memory")  # open_browser=True to open it

One self-contained file (no CDN, no server) with three tabs:

  • Disk: the Poincaré disk; hover a point for its text, id, level, depth, time, weight and parent; click to highlight ancestors and descendants; drag to pan hyperbolically (a Möbius translation); the time slider re-weights every memory under the configured policy and sets opacity accordingly; a text filter dims non-matches; "download JSON" exports the drawing data.
  • Table: sortable columns; clicking a row selects the memory in the disk.
  • Tree: the hierarchy as collapsible nodes with depth and weight.

docs.title: Layouts
docs.text: layout="structural" (default when parents exist) draws a radial tree: angles come from the hierarchy (each subtree owns a wedge proportional to its leaves) and radii from each memory's true hyperbolic depth. It is a drawing for reading, not an isometric embedding. layout="projection" draws the actual semantic directions reduced to 2-D (uncentred SVD of the tangent vectors at the origin, depths preserved); in high dimensions it tends to bunch memories, which is why it is not the default.

docs.title: Jupyter
docs.text: A Memory object renders the inspector inline (_repr_html_).

docs.title: Matplotlib
docs.text:
ax = mem.plot(labels=True)  # pip install "poincare-memory[viz]"
ax.figure.savefig("memory.png", dpi=160)

docs.title: Text views
docs.text:
print(mem.tree())  # ASCII tree with depths
rows = mem.table()  # list of dicts
df = mem.to_dataframe()  # pip install "poincare-memory[pandas]"
print(mem.stats())  # counts, levels, depths, timestamps, mean weight

docs.title: Exporting the drawing
docs.text: poincare_memory.viz.to_dict(mem) returns the nodes (with 2-D coordinates), edges and configuration the inspector uses; to_networkx(mem) builds a networkx.DiGraph with the same attributes.

docs.title: SQLite
docs.text:
from poincare_memory import Memory
from poincare_memory.demo import build_demo_memory

mem = build_demo_memory()
mem.save("memory.db")
mem2 = Memory.load("memory.db")
assert mem2.ids == mem.ids

save writes one file with the configuration, every record, its point and its embedding. load restores the hashing embedder and the built-in temporal policies automatically; if you used another embedder, pass the same one again (Memory.load(path, embedder=my_embedder)), and the dimension is checked.

docs.title: JSON
docs.text:
text = mem.to_json()  # portable, human-readable
mem.to_json("memory.json", indent=1)
mem3 = Memory.from_json("memory.json")

JSON is the format to use for sharing a memory, versioning it in git, or moving it between machines; SQLite is faster for large stores.

docs.title: From the command line
docs.text:
poincare-memory export memory.db memory.json
poincare-memory import memory.json memory.db
poincare-memory stats memory.db

docs.title: Format version
docs.text: Files carry a format number. A newer library refuses files it cannot read with a clear error rather than guessing.

docs.title: The index
docs.text:
The default search compares the query with every memory on the reference shell, which is fine to tens of thousands of memories. Beyond that, build an index:

from poincare_memory.demo import build_demo_memory

mem = build_demo_memory()
mem.build_index()  # NumPy by default; FAISS when installed
hits = mem.search("calf strain", k=5)

Once built, nearest searches with the shell metric take the k * oversample closest candidates from the index and score only those exactly (temporal policy, filters, depth bias). The index is marked stale on every change and rebuilt automatically on the next search; call build_index() yourself after a bulk load to control when that happens.

Backend Install Behaviour numpy none exact maximum inner product, vectorised faiss pip install "poincare-memory[ann]" HNSW with inner-product metric, approximate, millions of points

docs.title: Why a dot product is enough
docs.text:
Points on the ball map to the Lorentz model (PoincareBall.to_lorentz), where the distance is \(d = \operatorname{arcosh}(-c\,\langle X, Y\rangle_L)\), a decreasing function of the Lorentzian inner product. Negating the time coordinate of every stored vector (to_mips_vectors) turns \(\langle X, Y\rangle_L\) into an ordinary dot product, so any maximum-inner-product index returns exact hyperbolic nearest neighbours. No custom metric is needed in Qdrant, Milvus, Weaviate, pgvector, LanceDB or FAISS.

import numpy as np
from poincare_memory import PoincareBall, to_mips_vectors

ball = mem.ball
shell = ball.set_depth(mem.points, mem.base_depth)  # what the shell metric compares
stored = to_mips_vectors(ball.to_lorentz(shell))  # put these in your dot-product index
q = ball.to_lorentz(mem.embed_query("calf strain"))  # query with the raw Lorentz vector
scores = stored @ q  # larger = closer
top = np.argsort(-scores)[:5]

Store stored with the memory ids as payload; at query time take the top candidates from the database and let Memory score them with the temporal policy.

docs.title: Costs
docs.text: Placement is O(level) per add; add_many embeds in one batch. Exact search is O(n · dim). Memory per point is dim float64 for the point plus dim for the embedding.

docs.title: Structural queries
docs.text:
Flat vector stores answer one question: what is similar to this text. A hyperbolic memory also answers where things sit.

Mode Candidates Needs root Needs query nearest (default) every memory no yes subtree root and all its descendants yes optional children direct children of root yes optional ancestors parent, grandparent, … of root yes optional siblings other children of root's parent yes optional cone memories inside the entailment cone of root yes optional

Without a query, candidates are ranked by temporal weight and depth_bias only.

from poincare_memory import Memory
from poincare_memory.demo import build_demo_memory

mem = build_demo_memory()
print([r.id for r in mem.search("knee extension", mode="subtree", root="lower", k=3)])
print([r.id for r in mem.search(mode="ancestors", root="type2x")])
print([r.id for r in mem.search(mode="siblings", root="hams")])

docs.title: Combining with filters
docs.text:
filters is a dict of metadata equalities or a callable on the record, applied before ranking:

events = mem.search("hamstring", k=5, filters={"kind": "event"})
recent = mem.search("hamstring", k=5, filters=lambda r: r.access_count == 0)

docs.title: Zooming with depth_bias
docs.text:
general = mem.search("calf", k=3, touch=False)  # depth_bias = 0
mem.depth_bias = 0.5  # prefer deeper, more specific memories
specific = mem.search("calf", k=3, touch=False)
mem.depth_bias = 0.0

Positive depth_bias prefers specific memories, negative prefers general ones; it is a per-memory setting you can change between calls.

docs.title: Entailment cones
docs.text: mode="cone" is the geometric version of "everything this memory implies". With the default placement, cones are approximate (children are pulled only partly toward their parents); with Memory(cone_constrained=True) every child is forced inside its parent's cone and cone queries become exact for the declared hierarchy, at the cost of collapsing semantic directions. SearchResult.cone_energy is 0 inside the cone and grows with the violation angle.

docs.title: Time and forgetting
docs.text: Every memory carries a timestamp t (default: now, in UTC) and optional valid_from / valid_until. A temporal policy turns those into a weight in \((0, 1]\) at query time; the policy is a constructor argument of Memory.

docs.title: Half-life
docs.text:
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
from poincare_memory import HalfLife, Memory, generative_agents_recency

now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
mem = Memory(decay=HalfLife(hours=24 * 14))
mem.add("Calf tightness after hill sprints", id="a", t=now - timedelta(days=28))
mem.add("Completed 6 x 300 m at 95 %, felt strong", id="b", t=now - timedelta(days=1))
for r in mem.search("training this week", k=2):
    print(r.id, round(r.time_weight, 3))

A memory 28 days old under a 14-day half-life has weight 0.25. generative_agents_recency() is the \(0.995^{\text{hours}}\) recency of Generative Agents expressed as a half-life of about 138 hours.

docs.title: Ebbinghaus with access strengthening
docs.text:
from poincare_memory import Ebbinghaus

mem = Memory(decay=Ebbinghaus(stability_hours=24 * 7, boost_per_access=0.5))

Weight is \(e^{-\Delta t / S}\) with \(S = \text{stability\_hours}\cdot(1 + \text{boost\_per\_access}\cdot\text{accesses})\). Every time search returns a memory it increments the memory's access_count (disable with touch=False), so frequently retrieved memories decay more slowly.

docs.title: Validity windows for facts that stop being true
docs.text:
from poincare_memory import Product, ValidityWindow

mem = Memory(decay=Product(HalfLife(hours=24 * 90), ValidityWindow()))
mem.add(
    "API rate limit is 100 rps (release 2.3)",
    id="old",
    t=now - timedelta(days=90),
    valid_until=now - timedelta(days=20),
)
mem.add(
    "API rate limit is 250 rps (release 2.4)",
    id="new",
    t=now - timedelta(days=20),
    valid_from=now - timedelta(days=20),
)
print([r.id for r in mem.search("rate limit", k=2)])  # ['new', 'old']
print(
    [r.id for r in mem.search("rate limit", k=2, at_time=now - timedelta(days=40))]
)  # ['old', 'new']

Outside its window a memory keeps a tiny weight (outside_weight, default \(10^{-6}\)) rather than disappearing, so it can still be found when nothing else matches; filter it out explicitly if you want it gone (filters=lambda r: ...).

docs.title: How weight enters the score
docs.text: score = -distance + depth_bias * depth + time_coef * log(weight). With time_coef=1, a halving of the weight costs \(\ln 2 \approx 0.69\) score units, the same as a memory being 0.69 hyperbolic units further away. Set time_coef higher to let recency dominate, or 0 to ignore time while keeping the timestamps for inspection.

docs.title: Asking about the past
docs.text: search(at_time=some_datetime) evaluates the policy at that moment, which is how an agent can reconstruct what it would have retrieved on a given day. The inspector's time slider does the same visually.
